title: Mutation and aliases

sources.locator: CS2023 Software Development Fundamentals; August 2023; section applicable to Mutation and aliases
sources.claim: Rebinding changes which value a name denotes, while mutation changes the state of an existing mutable object that may be reachable through more than one name.

canonicalExplanation.summary: There are two different ways to "change" things. **Rebinding** (`x = something_new`) points one name at a different value. **Mutation** (`items.append(...)`) changes an existing object in place — and if two names refer to that same object (they are **aliases**), both see the change.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
You and a flatmate share a shopping list on the fridge. You write "milk" on it; later your flatmate reads the same list and sees milk — because it's one list with two readers. Code works the same way: two names refer to the same shopping-list object, so appending through one name makes the added item visible when reading through the other. In this lesson you'll predict visible changes when two names refer to the same mutable collection.

```predict
{"code": "ours = [\"eggs\"]\nmine = ours\nmine.append(\"milk\")\nprint(ours)", "question": "What does this print?", "options": ["[\"eggs\"]", "[\"eggs\", \"milk\"]"], "answer": 1, "why": "`mine = ours` doesn't copy the list — both names refer to **one** list. Appending through `mine` changes it for `ours` too."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Pseudocode** and **Variables and assignment** — especially that assignment binds a name to a value.

sections.heading: The distinction: rebinding vs mutation
sections.body:
| Code | Kind | Effect on the other name |
|---|---|---|
| `mine.append("milk")` | mutation. | visible through `ours` too. |
| `mine[0] = "bread"` | mutation. | visible through `ours` too. |
| `mine = ["tea"]` | rebinding. | `ours` unchanged — `mine` now points elsewhere. |

Numbers and strings can't be mutated, so this surprise only happens with **mutable** objects like lists, dicts and sets.

```reveal
{"prompt": "After `mine = [\"tea\"]`, what does `ours` hold?", "answer": "Still the shared list — `[\"eggs\", \"milk\"]`. Rebinding moved only the `mine` name to a brand-new list."}
```

sections.heading: Making a real copy
sections.body:
```predict
{"question": "How do you give `mine` its own independent list?", "options": ["`mine = ours`", "`mine = ours.copy()`"], "answer": 1, "why": "`.copy()` (or `list(ours)`) creates a new list with the same items. Now mutating one doesn't affect the other."}
```

Tip: `a is b` tells you whether two names are aliases of the same object.

examples.title: The shared shopping list
examples.situation: Two names refer to the same shopping-list object; appending through one name makes the added item visible when reading through the other.
walkthrough: **Alias:** `mine = ours` makes both names refer to the same shopping-list object.
**Mutate:** `mine.append("milk")` changes that one object in place.
**Read through the other name:** `print(ours)` shows the added item, milk.
examples.result: `ours` prints ["eggs", "milk"] — the added item is visible through both names.

examples.title: The default that remembered
examples.situation:
```python
template = ["name", "email"]
form_a = template
form_a.append("phone")
form_b = template
```
Form B was supposed to have only name and email.
walkthrough: `form_a` and `template` are aliases, so appending phone mutated the template.
`form_b = template` then aliases the already-changed list.
Fix: `form_a = template.copy()` so each form gets its own list.
examples.result: Form B wrongly includes phone until each form uses a copy of the template.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Assigning or updating through one name can never affect a value observed through another name.
misconceptions.correction: If two names refer to the same mutable object, mutating it through one name is visible through the other. Only rebinding a name, or working on a copy, keeps them independent.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The default that remembered", why did form B include phone?

analogy.example: Aliases are like **two people with the same shared Google Doc link**: edits by one appear for the other. Making a copy is "File → Make a copy" — now edits stay separate.
usefulFor: remembering that aliases share one object
seeing copy as the way to separate them
limitations: Numbers and strings can't be edited in place, so they never surprise you this way.
A shallow copy of a list of lists still shares the inner lists.

steps.explanation: A single shopping-list object is created and named ours.
Assigning mine = ours makes two names refer to the same object.
Appending through mine makes the added item visible when reading ours.

trace.textAlternative: Two names sharing one shopping list. Step 1, One object: ours is ['eggs']. A single shopping-list object is created and named ours. Step 2, Alias: mine is same object as ours. Assigning mine = ours makes two names refer to the same object. Step 3, Mutate: ours is ['eggs', 'milk']. Appending through mine makes the added item visible when reading ours.

remediation.explanation: Draw each object as a box and each name as an arrow. `=` moves an arrow; `.append` or `[i] =` changes what's inside a box. Any arrow to that box sees the change.
remediation.retryPrompt: Draw boxes and arrows for "The default that remembered".

recap.summary: To predict visible changes, check whether two names refer to the same mutable collection. Mutation (append, item assignment) changes the shared object, so both names see it; rebinding moves only one name. Use `.copy()` for independence.
retrievalPrompts: What's the difference between mutation and rebinding?
How do you give a name its own list?
